content: Your doctor has prescribed cefuroxime, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication can be administered either by injection into a large muscle, such as the buttock or hip, or through an intravenous (IV) infusion. The IV infusion involves adding the drug to a fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter over a 30-minute period, two to four times daily. Cefuroxime works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including those affecting the lungs, skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, and urinary tract. In some cases, cefuroxime may be prescribed for conditions not listed here; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through physical examinations and laboratory tests. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting cefuroxime, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to cefuroxime, other cephalosporins, penicillins, or any other medications. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, including other antibiotics, probenecid (Benemid), and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal diseases, particularly colitis. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Should you become pregnant while taking cefuroxime, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and routinely check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape for testing, as cefuroxime may cause false-positive results with Clinitest tablets. Before administering cefuroxime, inspect the solution carefully. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it or observing it closely. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. Follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop your treatment prematurely, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. Cefuroxime may cause side effects. If the medication is injected into a muscle, it may be mixed with lidocaine (Xylocaine) to minimize pain at the injection site. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following minor side effects, especially if they are severe or persistent: diarrhea, stomach pain, upset stomach, or vomiting. However, if you experience any of the following severe side effects, contact your healthcare provider immediately: unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, itching, rash, hives, or a sore mouth or throat. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving cefuroxime intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of medication at a time. Store the medication in the refrigerator or freezer as instructed. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator one hour in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are storing additional doses in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving cefuroxime intramuscularly, follow your healthcare provider’s storage instructions carefully. Keep all medications and supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving cefuroxime intravenously or subcutaneously, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection, which can occur at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms near the catheter site: tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain. Cefuroxime is available under the brand names Ceftin® and Zinacef®.
